summary: Defines NATV2-MIB, a Management Information Base module for monitoring Network Address Translator instances. It is meant to replace NAT-MIB from RFC 4008 and is not backwards compatible.

eli5.summary: This is a checklist of dials and gauges for watching a network address translator, a newer version of an older checklist.

questions: how to monitor nat with snmp
subtitle: A rewritten SNMP MIB for watching NAT devices, built around state, counters and early-warning notifications.

tldr.problem: The earlier NAT-MIB (RFC 4008) did not fit existing NAT implementations and was not much implemented, and it could not describe carrier-grade NAT with many subscribers, realms and NAT instances.
tldr.mechanism: NATV2-MIB is a new MIB module that mostly exposes read-only state and statistics for NAT instances, subscribers, protocols and address pools, plus a few writable resource limits and notification thresholds.
tldr.outcome: It is meant to replace NAT-MIB and is not backwards compatible with it. It defines compliance levels for basic NAT, pooled NAT and carrier-grade NAT.

today: RFC 7659 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated. It is intended to replace the NAT-MIB module in RFC 4008, and the abstract says a companion document deprecates all objects in NAT-MIB.

sections.title: Why a New NAT MIB
sections.content:
RFC 7659 defines NATV2-MIB, a Management Information Base (MIB) module for monitoring devices that perform Network Address Translation. A MIB is a set of managed objects that are normally read through SNMP, and this one is written in SMIv2.

It supersedes NAT-MIB from RFC 4008, which the text says did not fit well with existing NAT implementations and so was not much implemented. RFC 7658 gives the detailed analysis of those deficiencies.

Compared with RFC 4008, the new module removes nearly all writable configuration (only notification control and resource quotas stay), exposes only the read-only configuration needed as context, drops the link between mappings and interfaces, refers to NAT behaviors from RFC 4787 instead of NAT types, and uses standard IANA protocol numbers instead of its own list. It adds protective limits, more state and statistics, support for carrier-grade NAT (CGN) with subscribers, many address realms and several NAT instances on one device, richer address pools, and a port map indexing that makes tracing a packet back to an internal host easier.
sections.eli5: The old checklist did not match how real mailrooms worked, so nobody used it. This is a new checklist that mostly lets you look at the dials instead of turning them.

sections.title: The Tables and Indexes
sections.content:
The module organizes its objects into tables. Four textual conventions identify things: ProtocolNumber (an IANA protocol number), Natv2SubscriberIndex, Natv2InstanceIndex and Natv2PoolIndex. Index values are administered and meant to stay permanently tied to what they name. The subscriber index is scoped to the device, not the NAT instance, so subscribers can be moved between instances for load balancing.

  • Subscriber table: one row per subscriber, with its internal address or prefix and address realm, state, statistics and per-subscriber limits.
  • Instance table: one row per NAT instance, with its port mapping, filtering, pooling and fragment behaviors from RFC 4787, plus instance-wide limits, thresholds and counters.
  • Protocol table: per-protocol state and statistics. Supported protocols MUST include ICMP(1), TCP(6), UDP(17) and ICMPv6(58).
  • Pool table and pool range table: address pools, their realm, address type, port range and the address ranges they hold.
  • Address map table: current internal-to-external address mappings.
  • Port map table: current mappings by protocol from external realm, address and port to the internal ones. The indexing is designed so a session can be traced back to the host from packets seen in the external realm.

For Dual-Stack Lite (RFC 6333), the address and realm used for indexing are those of the outer IPv6 header, and the inner IPv4 source address, in the 192.0.0.0/29 range, is held in extra objects.
sections.eli5: Think of a set of notebooks: one lists the customers, one the mailrooms, one the stamps in use, and one which outside address stands for which inside address. Each notebook has a label so you can look things up fast.

sections.title: State, Statistics and Limits
sections.content:
State information is a snapshot of the mapping tables: the current number of address map entries and port map entries, reported per NAT instance, per protocol, per address pool and per subscriber. Address map entries are not counted per protocol because address mapping does not depend on protocol.

Counters are cumulative from a recorded discontinuity time. They include translations, address and port map entry creations (static mappings included), and several kinds of drops: address map limit drops, port map limit drops, active subscriber limit drops, address mapping failure drops, port mapping failure drops, fragment drops and other resource drops. The module takes care to let an address mapping failure be told apart from a port mapping failure.

Writable limits protect the device. When a limit is reached, packets that would need more of that resource are dropped instead of translated, and a counter records it. Limits cover address map entries and port map entries per instance, held fragments (relevant when a NAT can accept out-of-order fragments, per RFC 4787), active subscribers per instance, and port map entries per subscriber.
sections.eli5: The gauges count how many letters were handled and how many were thrown away, and why. Safety limits say that when the mailroom is full, new letters are turned away instead of jamming everything.

sections.title: Notifications
sections.content:
NATV2-MIB provides five notifications that warn of the need to add or reallocate NAT resources. Each has a writable threshold and a writable rate control, and all are disabled by default: a threshold of -1 disables a notification.

  • natv2NotificationPoolUsageHigh and natv2NotificationPoolUsageLow: pool usage, measured as the percentage of allocated ports in use for the most-mapped protocol, reaches an upper threshold or falls to a lower one.
  • natv2NotificationInstanceAddressMapEntriesHigh and natv2NotificationInstancePortMapEntriesHigh: the total number of address or port map entries in the instance reaches the threshold.
  • natv2NotificationSubscriberPortMapEntriesHigh: a subscriber's port map entries reach its threshold.

The RFC separates triggering (recognizing the event) from reporting (sending the message), because rate controls can delay or suppress a report.
sections.eli5: The warning lights come on when a room is nearly full, or nearly empty, so someone can fix it before letters get lost. They start switched off.

sections.title: Three Conformance Levels
sections.content:
The conformance statements cover three application scenarios. A basic NAT MAY limit itself to one NAT instance and two realms, though it MUST support indexing by instance, and it need not implement the subscriber, pool or pool range tables. A NAT supporting address pools adds the pool and pool range tables and MUST support more than two realms. A CGN MUST support the full module, including the subscriber table and the DS-Lite handling in the address and port map tables.

Object identifiers sit under natv2MIB, assigned in the mib-2 tree. It has four groups: notifications (0), device objects (1), instance objects (2) and conformance (3).
sections.eli5: A small shop needs only a few gauges, a bigger shop needs more, and a huge city-wide post office needs all of them.

sections.title: Operating It and Moving from NAT-MIB
sections.content:
The MIB assumes the realms, subscriber information, NAT instances, behaviors, supported protocols, pool details and static mappings are configured by other means. The RFC says it was written before practical experience with setting limits and thresholds, so it gives only general principles.

For thresholds, the operator should weigh how volatile usage is and how long mitigation takes. The worked example is usage growing 1% a week with 10% hourly variation and two weeks needed to act: set the threshold to 88% of the limit, or 90% if action is immediate. Default notification intervals run from 10 seconds for address and port map thresholds to 60 seconds for per-subscriber thresholds.

On coexistence with RFC 4008, the RFC notes that NAT-MIB is mainly about configuration while NATV2-MIB is mainly about measurements. Their counters and state values differ in granularity and model, so only coarse comparisons, such as total translations or total discards per NAT instance after aggregation, are possible.
sections.eli5: Set the warning light early enough that you have time to fetch more room, but not so early that it keeps beeping. The old and new checklists count things differently, so you can only compare their grand totals.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Writable objects are sensitive. An attacker who sets a very low or very high limit can cause denial of service. An arbitrarily low threshold can cause useless notifications, and an arbitrarily high one can effectively disable them, which could hide another attack. A low interval combined with a low threshold also floods notifications.

Readable objects can reveal private host identities, notably entries in the subscriber, address map and port map tables, which also raises subscriber privacy concerns. Other objects expose NAT capabilities, policies and state. The RFC says no object is sensitive like a password or a monetary amount.

Implementations SHOULD provide the SNMPv3 security features, and deploying SNMP versions before SNMPv3 is NOT RECOMMENDED. Operators must configure the SNMP entity so only legitimate principals can GET or SET these objects.
sections.eli5: The dials that change settings and the lists of who is talking to whom should only be touched or seen by people you trust, so lock the control room.
